sections.html:
McClain County is a south central Oklahoma county on the southern edge of the Oklahoma City metro, with Purcell as the seat. Population in 2020 was 41,662, spread over 16,421 housing units. Owners occupy about 79.8 percent of the occupied homes, and 7.2 percent of units stood empty. That is a market of regular family houses.

Blanchard, Newcastle and Purcell are the cities. Smaller towns include Byars, Cole, Dibble, Goldsby, Maysville, Rosedale, Washington and Wayne. Your bill is the sum of three layers: the county, whichever city or town you live in, and the school district. Districts such as Alex, Asher, Blanchard, Bridge Creek, Dibble, Lindsay, Maysville, Newcastle, Norman, Paoli, Purcell, Stratford, Washington and Wayne each set their own levy, so a pair of equally valued houses can get different bills if a district line runs between them.

Interstate 35 is the main road, and commute time is usually the first thing a buyer asks.

Property tax here is run by two elected offices. The assessor decides what your property is worth and builds the roll. The treasurer sends the bills, takes payments and distributes the money to the county, the cities and towns, and the schools. Both sit in Purcell.

Online, oktaxrolls.com lets you search the roll and pay. The assessor's desk also handles records and maps, exemption applications and a four-year cycle of visual property inspections, and it staffs the board that corrects the roll. Current details are on the McClain County Assessor page and the treasurer page.

sections.h2: How a tax bill is built
sections.html:
Here is the sequence. Values go from the assessor to the County Equalization Board and then the State Board of Equalization. The Excise Board certifies millage rates. Then the assessor builds the roll and hands it to the treasurer, who mails the bills. A mill equals $1 of tax on every $1,000 of taxable value. Statewide, assessment ratios sit between 10 and 15 percent, and total mill rates commonly land between 90 and 110.

Because each government sets its own levy, no two neighborhoods are guaranteed the same rate. Look at the school district named on the bill rather than borrowing a neighbor's figure.

  • Value: the assessor, with a visual inspection of each property every four years.
  • Levy: the taxing bodies, certified by the Excise Board.
  • Billing: the treasurer, once the finished roll is filed.

The first installment does not go delinquent until 30 days after the assessor files the completed rolls with the treasurer.

Bills become payable on November 1. You can split the payment: the first half is needed before January 1 and the second half before April 1. Skip the first half and the entire amount becomes delinquent on January 1.

  • A balance of $25 or less has to be paid in one piece before January 1.
  • Interest on late tax runs 1.5 percent each month and stops when it matches the unpaid tax.
  • Mortgage servicers make one annual payment ahead of January 1.
  • The treasurer can waive a penalty or interest when the delay was not the taxpayer's fault.

Closing between November and March? Ask the treasurer's office whether the first half is in. A current account closes cleanly, while a delinquent one needs a payoff figure, and the title company will ask for it early.

Your first step is a written protest sent to the assessor. If the county mailed a notice of increased valuation, the clock is 30 calendar days from that mailing date. When the value stayed the same, you have until the first Monday in April.

Next comes an informal hearing, and the assessor owes you a written decision within 7 calendar days. Unhappy with it? You get 15 calendar days from the date that decision was mailed to take the case to the county board of equalization. Attach the valuation information the form asks for, since a protest missing it leaves the assessor's number presumed correct.

Gather comparable sales, repair bids and photos of damage before you file. A protest with paper behind it gets a better hearing than a general complaint.

sections.h2: Homestead exemption and the 3 percent cap
sections.html:
A primary residence qualifies for a $1,000 homestead exemption against taxable value, and its assessed value can climb no more than 3 percent a year while you own it. You apply at the assessor's office.

When the house sells, the cap resets. The next owner's first bill can come in higher than yours, so tell any buyer who is budgeting from your numbers. The exemption follows the person who lives in the home, which means a buyer files a fresh application after the deed is recorded.

If tax is unpaid when you sell, it comes out of your proceeds at closing, and the title company gets the payoff amount from the treasurer. Delinquent city charges for weeds, cleanup, paving or nuisance abatement are certified to the treasurer and attach to the parcel as a lien, so ask about them too.

A parcel left unpaid for long enough ends up in the annual delinquent-tax sale, and the treasurer then manages the county-owned property. If you are behind, or you inherited a house with back taxes, learn the real payoff before you decide anything.

  1. Search the parcel on oktaxrolls.com and write down every year that shows a balance.
  2. Phone the treasurer and ask for a written payoff that includes interest.
  3. Ask the city whether any weed or cleanup charges were certified.
  4. Pass the figures to the title company so your closing statement shows the true net.

Plan the paperwork before the buyer does. Early in the process, pull the parcel record and see which tax years are open. In the second week, ask the assessor whether a homestead exemption or any correction is pending on the account. Once you have a contract, the title company orders its own payoff, and any city lien surfaces then. Closing day is when the county gets paid out of your proceeds, so nothing carries over to the buyer.

A cash offer shortens this because there is no lender appraisal or underwriting queue. You still need clear title, so the tax and lien research is the same either way. If the house sits in a different school district than a neighbor's, say so up front, because buyers who ask about taxes tend to ask about schools in the same breath.

Typical sellers inherited a house, put off repairs, own a rental with a tenant inside, or carry back taxes. About one in five occupied homes in the county is rented, so landlords are a normal part of the picture.

A fast cash sale appeals to people who would rather skip showings, inspection haggling and a lender's repair list. Condition varies by area: rural parcels near the Canadian and Washita rivers, hilly lots in the west and older homes in Purcell and Byars all raise their own repair questions. Selling as-is means you leave those fixes to the buyer. Before choosing any route, get taxes and city liens in writing so you know the net.

What to have ready when you call a buyer or the title company: the parcel number, your latest tax bill, any notice of valuation, the deed or probate paperwork if the house was inherited, and a list of known repairs.

faqs.q: Who sets the value of my McClain County home?
faqs.a: The County Assessor does. The office is at 121 N. 2nd Ave, Room 206 in Purcell and the phone is 405-527-3520.

faqs.q: When does McClain County want property tax paid?
faqs.a: Bills are payable November 1. Half must be in before January 1 to avoid delinquency on the whole levy, and the other half is due before April 1.

faqs.q: What does a late payment cost?
faqs.a: Interest builds at 1.5 percent a month on delinquent tax. It stops once the interest equals the unpaid tax.

faqs.q: What is my deadline to dispute a value?
faqs.a: Thirty calendar days from the mailing date of an increase notice. With no change in value, the protest is due the first Monday in April.

faqs.q: Will back taxes stop me from selling?
faqs.a: No. The balance is paid out of your proceeds at closing, and the treasurer can give the title company a payoff figure.
